title: Pulling a divisor identity back by a holomorphic map
notes: For a positive line bundle with \(c(L)=\omega\) and \(D=\{\sigma=0\}\), the notes write \(d[\eta]-[\omega]=[D]\) and the same formula after pullback by \(f\).
statement: Let \(L\to V\) have a smooth Hermitian metric with positive curvature form \(\omega=c_1(L,h)\), and let \(f:\mathbb C^n\to V\) have image not contained in the zero divisor \(D\) of \(\sigma\). The pullback section \(f^*\sigma\) defines \(D_f=f^*D\), with multiplicity, and \(dd^c\log\|f^*\sigma\|^2=[D_f]-f^*\omega\). Thus \([D_f]=dd^c\log\|f^*\sigma\|^2+f^*\omega\). This is justified by applying Poincaré--Lelong to the pullback section, not by assuming that every current has a pullback under every map.
fate: \citet[Proposition 1.14 and Section 5(b)]{griffithsking1973nevanlinna} gives precisely the identity used in the first main theorem. The minus sign in the notebook's rearranged formula conflicts with its correct formula on P000599.
present_status: As of November 2026: established in the stated scope; the notebook is an expository occurrence, not a new open problem.

title: The missing boundary term in the counting calculation
notes: After multiplication by \(\chi_{B(r)}\varphi^{n-1}\), a displayed integral over apparently \(S(r)\) of \(\varphi^{n-1}\wedge f^*\omega\) is equated to divisor volume.
statement: For almost every radius, the current identity gives \(\int_{D_f\cap B(r)}\omega_0^{n-1}=\int_{B(r)}f^*\omega\wedge\omega_0^{n-1}+\int_{S(r)}d^c\log\|f^*\sigma\|^2\wedge\omega_0^{n-1}\), interpreted by smooth approximation if needed. The first integral is over the ball, while the boundary integral has degree \(2n-1\) and contains the logarithmic derivative. Integrating the \(2n\)-form \(f^*\omega\wedge\omega_0^{n-1}\) over a sphere is dimensionally inappropriate.
reconstruction: The sign follows the fixed ddc convention; the stated identity supplies the missing Stokes term.
fate: This is the Stokes step in the twice-integrated Poincaré--Lelong argument of \citet[Proposition 5.11 and its reference to Section 3]{griffithsking1973nevanlinna}. The notebook has suppressed the essential boundary term; the faint domain letter does not repair that omission.
present_status: As of November 2026: established in the stated scope; the notebook is an expository occurrence, not a new open problem.

title: Integrated divisor counting and the radius exponent
notes: The notes pass from raw divisor volume to \(N(D_f,r)=\int_0^r(\int_{D_f\cap B(\rho)}\varphi^{n-1})\,d\rho/\rho^{n+1}\), while the preceding line uses the classical \(d\rho/\rho\) notation.
statement: Use ordinary Euclidean radius, \(\omega_0=(i/2)\sum_jdz_j\wedge d\bar z_j\), and \(dd^c=(i/2\pi)\partial\bar\partial\). Set \(n_D(t)=\int_{D_f\cap B(t)}\omega_0^{n-1}\). For fixed \(r_0>0\) and \(r\ge r_0\), define \(N_f(D,r)=\pi^{1-n}\int_{r_0}^r n_D(t)t^{-(2n-1)}\,dt\) and \(T_f(r)=\pi^{1-n}\int_{r_0}^r(\int_{B(t)}f^*\omega\wedge\omega_0^{n-1})t^{-(2n-1)}\,dt\). For \(n=1\), the weight is \(dt/t\). Equivalently one normalizes the raw masses by \(t^{2n-2}\) and then integrates with \(dt/t\).
reconstruction: The Euclidean form, ordinary radius, base radius, and factor \(\pi^{1-n}\) are fixed editorially. They follow from \(\int_{B(t)}dd^c u\wedge\omega_0^{n-1}=(\pi^{n-1}/2)t^{2n-1}(d/dt)\operatorname{Avg}_{S(t)}u\); this independently checks the dimension-one reduction.
fate: The counting and characteristic definitions used in \citet[Sections 3(a) and 5(b)]{griffithsking1973nevanlinna} have the Jensen radial normalization. The notebook's \(\rho^{n+1}\) is not the Euclidean-radius exponent \(2n-1\) (they happen to agree at \(n=2\)); it already fails the one-dimensional check.
present_status: As of November 2026: established in the stated scope; the notebook is an expository occurrence, not a new open problem.

title: The first main theorem bounds divisor counting by growth
notes: The final inequality is \(N(D_f,r)\le T(f,r)+O(1)\), called the first Nevanlinna inequality.
statement: For the compact Hermitian target and nonzero pullback section above, scale \(\sigma\) so that \(\|\sigma\|\le1\). With the definitions of 1974-360.17, put \(m_f(D,r)=\operatorname{Avg}_{S(r)}\log(1/\|f^*\sigma\|)\ge0\), where the average uses Euclidean surface probability measure. The integrated Poincaré--Lelong identity is \(N_f(D,r)+m_f(D,r)=T_f(r)+m_f(D,r_0)\). Therefore \(N_f(D,r)\le T_f(r)+O(1)\), with a constant depending on the section, metric, and fixed \(r_0\), but not on \(r\).
fate: \citet[Proposition 5.11 and equation (5.12), p.~184]{griffithsking1973nevanlinna} is the exact source, published in 1973, two years before this talk. This is an established first main theorem; no second-main-theorem or defect assertion is silently added. It connects thematically with the earlier Picard/Nevanlinna discussion 1965-71.1.
present_status: As of November 2026: established in the stated scope; the notebook is an expository occurrence, not a new open problem.

title: The first main inequality recalled with its constant suppressed
notes: The continuation repeats \(N(D_f,r)\le T(f,r)\) and labels an iterated integral the order of growth; its inner ball is written \(B(r)\) although the outer variable is \(t\).
statement: Under the hypotheses and compatible counting definitions of 1974-360.17--18, the invariant statement is \(N_f(D,r)\le T_f(r)+O(1)\). A chosen additive normalization of \(T_f\) may absorb the bounded term for a fixed divisor, but the term cannot simply be dropped for arbitrary normalizations. The inner ball in a radial growth integral is \(B(t)\), and raw ball masses require the dimension-dependent normalization described there.

title: The sign and normalization of the Ricci form of a volume
notes: First \(\operatorname{Ric}\Omega=i\partial\bar\partial\log g\) for \(\Omega=(i/2)g\,dz\wedge d\bar z\); then the general formula has \(i/(2\pi)\). The text says its scalar coefficient is minus Gaussian curvature.
statement: For a positive smooth volume form locally \(\Omega=a\,dV_{\mathrm{hol}}\), define \(R_\Omega=dd^c\log a=(i/2\pi)\partial\bar\partial\log a\). The form is invariant under holomorphic coordinate changes, because the logarithm of the Jacobian modulus squared is pluriharmonic. This is the negative of the usual normalized Ricci form. In one complex dimension, with metric area \(\Omega=(i/2)g\,dz\wedge d\bar z\) and Gaussian curvature \(K_g\), \(i\partial\bar\partial\log g=-K_g\Omega\), while \(R_\Omega=-K_g\Omega/(2\pi)\).
reconstruction: The notation R is editorial and makes explicit that the notebook uses the negative Ricci convention.
fate: The volume-form curvature convention and coordinate invariance are used in \citet[Section 2]{griffiths1971canonical}. The notebook has the correct negative-Gaussian sign, but shifts the normalization by \(2\pi\) between two displays; those displays must not be combined without that factor.
present_status: As of November 2026: established in the stated scope; the notebook is an expository occurrence, not a new open problem.

title: The volume-curvature inequalities needed for comparison
notes: The two explicit assumptions are \(\operatorname{Ric}\Omega>0\) and \((\operatorname{Ric}\Omega)^n\ge\Omega\).
statement: On a complex \(n\)-manifold with a positive \(C^2\) volume form \(\Omega\), assume \(R_\Omega\) is a positive definite real \((1,1)\)-form and \(R_\Omega^n\ge\Omega\) as positive top-degree forms, in the same \(dd^c\) convention. This determinant inequality fixes the necessary scale. Multiplication of \(\Omega\) by a positive constant leaves \(R_\Omega\) unchanged but changes the comparison inequality.
fate: \citet[Lemma 2.3 and the proof of Proposition 2.7]{griffiths1971canonical} supplies volume forms with such normalized curvature control in the canonical algebraic setting and the corresponding maximum-principle argument. The notebook's explicit analytic inequalities are more informative than its later shorthand 'negative curvature'.

title: Ahlfors-type volume decrease from the ball or polydisc
notes: With the Bergman volume on \(B^n\) or \(\Delta^n\), every holomorphic map to \(V^n\) with negatively curved volume satisfies \(f^*\Omega_V\le\Phi_B\).
statement: Normalize the complete invariant volume \(\Phi_U\) on the unit ball or polydisc \(U\) so that \(R_{\Phi_U}>0\) and \(R_{\Phi_U}^n=\Phi_U\). Let \(V\) have complex dimension \(n\). If a positive \(C^2\) volume form \(\Omega_V\) satisfies \(R_{\Omega_V}>0\) and \(R_{\Omega_V}^n\ge\Omega_V\), every holomorphic \(f:U\to V\) satisfies \(f^*\Omega_V\le\Phi_U\). At rank-deficient points the left side vanishes. The comparison follows by applying the maximum principle to the ratio \(f^*\Omega_V/\Phi_{U_s}\) on smaller balls or polydiscs \(U_s\) and letting \(s\) increase to one.
reconstruction: The analytic curvature inequalities explicitly stated in the notes are used as hypotheses; the checked publication has the canonical-algebraic target as its stated setting. This is a faithful proof reconstruction, not a claim of a new generalization.
fate: \citet[Proposition 2.7, pp.~444--445]{griffiths1971canonical}, received 27 March 1970 and published in May 1971, proves volume decrease for maps to complete canonical algebraic manifolds. Its proof gives the displayed analytic sufficient-condition version. The notebook's blanket curvature-\(-1\) description must be replaced by compatible source and target volume normalizations; the polydisc does not have constant holomorphic sectional curvature.
